items.title: Liu Lab Skills
items.text:
Agent Skills that teach AI coding agents how the Liu Lab works, starting with its HPC clusters. Built for Claude Code, and they work in any tool that reads the open skills standard.

Ask an agent to "run this on the cluster" and it needs lab knowledge it cannot guess: which clusters exist, how a job gets submitted, what is safe to do. This plugin holds that knowledge.

Skill What it covers lab-hpc The two clusters (arc/chimera GPU, ircbc CPU), Slurm, the safety rules, the per-machine setup check. lab-jupyter Jupyter Lab on a compute node, tunnelled to your local browser. lab-containers The lab's Singularity images on ircbc: keeping them current, running work inside them. lab-edison The Edison platform: Kosmos for a whole research goal, cited literature answers and data analysis for a single question. No cluster. lab-setup One step after installing: the plugin updates by itself, and Codex and Kimi Code get it too. hq-mode A whole task done the lab's way: working rules, a playbook per kind of task, and a list of steps that always wait for your yes.

The first three load by themselves when your request touches remote compute. You call the last three by name: lab-edison because every run of it costs you money, lab-setup because you need it once per machine, and hq-mode because you choose when a task gets it.

items.title: What the agent will not do
items.text:
It never runs compute on a login node, never submits a job you have not seen, and never picks a cluster in silence. On a machine that is not set up it refuses and points you at the setup below, rather than asking for an address or a password. When ircbc stops answering it tells you to check the VPN instead of retrying in a loop.

No secrets in this repo

The skills hold no hostnames, addresses, usernames or keys. Hosts appear only as ssh alias names, and the rest is read from your ~/.ssh/config at run time. That is what makes this repo safe to publish.

items.title: Install
items.text:
Two commands in your terminal:

claude plugin marketplace add liuhlab/liulab-skills
claude plugin install lab@liulab

Then start Claude Code and type /lab-setup. It turns on updates for the plugin, and sets up Codex and Kimi Code if you have them. It also points each agent at the lab's defaults: where issues go, which labels to use, and the safety rules for the clusters. It asks before each change, and it removes nothing. Its page has the details.

Then set the machine up for the clusters once.

  1. SSH aliases. Your ~/.ssh/config needs the lab's usual alias names: arc, chimera-login, chimera-transfer, chimera-gpu, chimera-cpu, the per-node aliases, ircbc, ircbc-transfer, and cpu01 through cpu08, each with your own username and key. Ask a lab member for a working example. This repo ships none.
  2. Personal config. Copy templates/personal.md to ~/.claude/lab/personal.md and fill in your usernames, directories and Jupyter defaults. Never commit it.
  3. Edison key and pixi, only for lab-edison. That skill needs pixi on your PATH. Then copy templates/edison.env to ~/.claude/lab/edison.env, paste your own key over the placeholder, and chmod 600 it. It sits beside personal.md, never inside it. Never commit it.

To check the result, ask Claude: "Am I set up for the lab HPC clusters?" The skill runs its preflight and reports per cluster.

items.title: Codex and Kimi Code
items.text:
/lab-setup sets both up from Claude Code, so there is nothing to install by hand. Codex gets the same plugin and checks for a new release each time it starts. Kimi Code reads the skills from the copy Claude Code keeps up to date. No other agent tool is supported.

lab-edison waits for you to type its name in all three. Claude Code and Kimi Code read that from its settings. Codex reads it from a small opt-out file the skill also ships, agents/openai.yaml.

items.title: Updating
items.text:
Once /lab-setup has run, there is nothing to do: each agent picks up a new release on its own. To update by hand:

claude plugin marketplace update liulab
claude plugin update lab@liulab

Claude Code loads plugins when it starts, so restart your session before the updated skills are there.

items.title: Moving from lab-compute
items.text:
Until 2026.10.1 this repo was liulab-compute-skills and the plugin was lab-compute. A plain update does not cross a rename, so do it by hand once:

claude plugin uninstall lab-compute@liulab
claude plugin marketplace remove liulab
claude plugin marketplace add liuhlab/liulab-skills
claude plugin install lab@liulab
mv ~/.claude/compute ~/.claude/lab

The last line moves your own files to where the skills now look for them. Every skill refuses to run while ~/.claude/compute is still there. If you installed from a clone instead, use the two commands under Install. /lab-setup then lists the links your old install left, for you to remove.

items.title: Basic usage
items.text:
First install the plugin with the two commands on the home page, then type /lab-setup once in Claude Code. From then on the skills keep themselves up to date, in Claude Code, Codex and Kimi Code alike.

Talk to your agent about cluster work and the right skill loads itself. In Claude Code you can also call one directly: /lab-hpc, or lab-jupyter, or lab-containers.

lab-edison is the exception. It never loads on its own, because every run spends your own credits. Ask for it by name.

items.title: Things you can ask
items.text:
"Test this repo on chimera." The agent moves your code the lab way, local to GitHub to a git pull on the cluster. It takes a compute node, never the login node, and runs the tests there. You see the exact sbatch or srun first.

"Get me a GPU node on chimera." It drafts a job on the lab's free zhoulab_gpu_priority partition and asks what you want: CPUs, memory, GPUs, time.

"Start Jupyter Lab on the cluster and open it on my laptop." lab-jupyter checks whether you already have a Jupyter job running, and reuses it. Otherwise it submits one with your approval, opens an ssh tunnel, and hands you a http://localhost:9990/lab?token=… link that works in your browser. Either cluster.

"Update the ml container image on ircbc." lab-containers compares your image's recorded digest against the registry and tells you whether an update is actually needed. Only then does it pull and rebuild, pulling on the login node and building in a job, because ircbc's compute nodes have no internet.

"Run this alignment on ircbc." The command runs inside the right lab container, in a Slurm job, with the environment active. The bare OS there is far too old for modern tools.

"/lab-edison what is known about …" lab-edison checks your key file, names the job it picked, prints your question in full, and only then sends it. You get an answer with citations, and the task id that paid for it. No cluster on this path.

For a goal too big for one question, ask about Kosmos. The skill drafts the goal with you and checks your data for free, and starts a run only when you ask for that run.

This is the one skill that wants a tool of its own: pixi on your PATH. Your first Edison command then builds what it runs in before it sends anything, so it can look hung. It is not. The build runs once more after each plugin update. See its page.

items.title: What the agent will ask you
items.text:
Which cluster, unless your request already makes it obvious. What the job needs: CPUs, memory, GPUs, wall time. And your confirmation of the exact command before any job is submitted.

It also asks before cancelling or deleting anything shared. Reservation jobs and container images belong to the whole group.

items.title: Tips
items.text:
Fill in ~/.claude/lab/personal.md with your Jupyter port, launch path and usual job resources, and the agent stops re-asking session after session.

Name the cluster in your request ("…on chimera", "…on ircbc") to skip the which-cluster question.

The skills tell the agent to read your ssh config, never to change it. SSH setup stays in your hands.

items.title: How the repo is organized
items.text: This section is for people who change the repo. The skill pages above are for people who use it. An agent working on the repo reads AGENTS.md instead. These pages explain the same rules for people.

items.title: One tree, read by every agent
items.text:
The repo root is the plugin. .claude-plugin/marketplace.json declares source: "./", so what you clone and what a lab member installs are the same files. Each agent tool reaches them by its own path:

flowchart TB
    repo["liuhlab/liulab-skills<br/>main branch"]
    repo -->|"git clone, kept on main"| clone["Claude Code's marketplace clone"]
    clone -->|"installs plugin lab@liulab"| cc["Claude Code"]
    clone -->|"reads the skills live"| kimi["Kimi Code"]
    repo -->|"its own git marketplace,<br/>upgraded at startup"| codex["Codex"]
    repo -->|"docs/ and mkdocs.yml"| site["This site, on GitHub Pages"]
    repo -->|"pixi run check"| ci["CI, on every pull request"]

Because the whole tree ships, nothing in it is private to developers. Tests, styles and these pages all land on every lab machine. That is why the repo's security rule covers every file, not only the skills.

items.title: Where things live
items.text:
liulab-skills/
├── .claude-plugin/       marketplace.json and plugin.json, which holds the version
├── skills/<name>/        one folder per skill: SKILL.md, references/, scripts/
├── src/edison_cli/       the Python package lab-edison spends credits through
├── bin/edison-cli        the command that runs it
├── upstream/             pins, attribution records and licenses for adopted skills
├── templates/            files a lab member copies to their own machine
├── tests/                lint.sh, preflight.sh, eval.sh and the pytest suite
├── scripts/              check.sh, conformance.py, upstream_sync.py
├── styles/Lab/           vale rules: word caps, jargon, reading grade
├── docs/                 this site, plus the unlisted adr/ and agents/ pages
├── .claude/commands/     the maintainer's upstream sync command
├── AGENTS.md             how an agent works on the repo (CLAUDE.md is a symlink to it)
├── GLOSSARY.md           the repo's words, one entry each
└── CHANGELOG.md          one entry per version

Two folders under docs/ hold pages for agents: docs/adr/ keeps the decision records, and docs/agents/ keeps the working rules. Both are built and reachable by URL, but they stay out of the menu and out of search.

items.title: Kinds of skill
items.text:
Every skill sits in one of a few kinds. The kind decides its name, who owns its text, and how it changes.

flowchart LR
    mode["hq-mode<br/>the mode"]
    mode -->|"sends each task to"| lab
    mode -->|"sends each task to"| adopted
    subgraph lab["Written by the lab: lab-* names"]
        direction TB
        recipes["lab-jupyter, lab-containers<br/>task recipes"] -->|"point at"| hpc["lab-hpc<br/>core skill"]
        typed["lab-edison, lab-setup<br/>typed by name"]
    end
    subgraph adopted["Adopted: upstream names kept"]
        direction TB
        tracked["Tracked<br/>from mattpocock/skills"]
        forked["Forked<br/>from pstack"]
    end
  • The core skill, lab-hpc, holds what is true about the clusters. Every other cluster skill points at it and never repeats it.
  • Task recipes hold one procedure each. lab-jupyter owns a Jupyter session from start to cleanup. lab-containers owns every command that runs inside a container, including the one lab-jupyter borrows on ircbc.
  • Typed-by-name skills never load on their own. lab-edison spends money and lab-setup changes a machine, so a person starts each one.
  • The mode, hq-mode, is a router. It picks a playbook for the task and sends the agent to the right skill at each step.
  • Adopted skills come from two outside projects. Upstream skills explains how each one arrives and changes.

The README's "Adding a new skill" section has the steps for a new one.

items.title: How a change ships
items.text:
Every merged change is a release, even one that only touches a test.

flowchart TB
    edit["Edit on a branch, run pixi run check"] --> bump["Bump plugin.json and add a CHANGELOG entry,<br/>in the same commit"]
    bump --> pr["Open a pull request: CI runs the same gate"]
    pr --> merge["Merge to main, tag main, push"]
    merge --> machines["Every agent takes the release at its next launch"]

Versions are calendar dates, YEAR.MONTH.PATCH, such as 2026.7.0. Design choices says why every change bumps one.

items.title: Checking a change
items.text:
pixi run check is the one command that must pass. It starts every check at once and reports every failure in a single run, so read the output to the bottom.

flowchart LR
    you["You, before you push"] --> check["pixi run check"]
    ci["CI, on every pull request"] -->|"same task, by name"| check
    check --> static["check-static, all at once:<br/>ruff, format, pyright, pytest, vale,<br/>markdownlint, shellcheck, conformance"]
    check --> lint["tests/lint.sh:<br/>manifests, skill names, no-secrets sweep,<br/>version tags, eval case lists"]

The list of steps lives in one place, the check-static task in pyproject.toml. CI calls that task by name, so your machine and CI cannot drift apart. To add a check, add it there.

Two more checks run only on your own machine, never in CI. tests/preflight.sh reads your real ssh config. tests/eval.sh runs a full agent session per case and costs tokens, so run one case with --only when a change to a skill's behavior needs proof.

items.title: The rules that hold everywhere
items.text:
• No connection details, ever. No addresses, hostnames, usernames, key names or passwords, in any file. Hosts appear only as the lab's ssh alias names. tests/lint.sh sweeps for leaks, using your own ssh config to know what to look for, so run the gate before you push.
  • Nothing runs on a cluster without a person's yes. A skill shows the exact job script and waits.
  • Agent text has word caps, and people's text has a reading grade. Design choices explains the split.

items.title: Design choices
items.text: The choices below shape most changes to this repo. Each one names what it costs, and links the decision record that argues it in full. The records live under docs/adr/. A choice that was later reversed links the record that reversed it.

items.title: One plugin, updated as a whole
items.text:
Every skill ships in one plugin, lab, from one marketplace, liulab. The skills lean on each other: lab-jupyter takes a job line word for word from lab-containers, and both defer to lab-hpc for the safety rules. A machine running two skills at two different versions is a mix nobody tests. That mix fails as a wrong command on a real cluster, which is the worst place to find out.

One plugin makes an update all or nothing. The cost is that a lab member who wants one skill installs all of them, and every skill's description takes a little of every agent's context. That pressure is why descriptions stay short and dense with trigger words.

Read the record: The repo root is the plugin, and one plugin holds every skill.

items.title: A version names one tree
items.text:
Every change merged to main bumps the version, even a change to a test or a comment. The whole tree ships, so two different trees must never answer to one number. tests/lint.sh fails a tagged version whose files have moved since the tag.

flowchart LR
    merge["A change merges to main"] --> ver["A new version,<br/>tagged on main after the merge"]
    ver --> cc["Claude Code:<br/>autoUpdate on the marketplace"]
    ver --> codex["Codex:<br/>upgrades at startup"]
    ver --> kimi["Kimi Code:<br/>reads Claude Code's clone"]

Versions are calendar dates, YEAR.MONTH.PATCH. What ships is prose an agent reads, with no API to break, so the only thing a version needs to say is how old a copy is.

Installed copies update on their own. Releasing is pushing, and a fixed safety rule reaches every machine at its next launch. So does a bad release, with nobody choosing to take it.

Read the records: The version names one tree, CalVer, and Installed copies update on their own, which reversed the manual-update half of the CalVer record.

items.title: Facts and procedures live apart
items.text:
New content goes where its kind says, not where the person asking for it happens to work.

flowchart LR
    q{"What are you<br/>adding?"}
    q -->|"how a cluster behaves"| a["skills/lab-hpc/references/<br/>checked on a compute node, dated"]
    q -->|"how a vendor platform behaves"| b["the owning skill's references/<br/>under a provenance block"]
    q -->|"a repeatable procedure"| c["its own lab-* skill,<br/>pointing at the facts"]
    q -->|"a one-line tip"| d["a bullet in lab-hpc"]
    q -->|"what a word means"| e["GLOSSARY.md"]
    q -->|"a hard-to-reverse decision"| f["docs/adr/"]
    q -->|"open work"| g["a GitHub issue"]

A fact copied into two skills goes stale in one of them, and no check can tell which copy is right. On a cluster that is not a stale sentence. It is an agent typing squeue --me on a Slurm version that lacks it.

Two rules keep facts honest:

  • Record configuration, never measurements. Configuration is what an agent must type: a partition's time limit, a port, a module name. A measurement is free disk space, a queue wait or a node count. It is true for one afternoon, and the agent cannot tell when it went stale. Write the guidance and the command that gives a live value instead: "/large_storage fills up, check df -h", not "81% used".
  • Facts carry their source. A vendor fact cannot be checked again for free, so each lab-edison reference page opens with a provenance block. The block gives its source, the date it was checked, and one of three tiers. Verified means we ran it. Read means it came from the package source or a vendor page. Unverified means it was inferred. Lint fails a page without one.

Read the records: Facts versus recipes, Jupyter and containers split at the job line, and Facts carry their provenance.

items.title: No secrets, by construction
items.text:
The repo is public, so it holds no connection details at all. Skills name hosts only by the lab's ssh alias names, and read everything else from the user's machine when they run.

flowchart LR
    subgraph pub["Public repo"]
        skill["Skill text<br/>alias names only:<br/>arc, ircbc, ..."]
    end
    subgraph mine["The user's machine, never committed"]
        direction TB
        ssh["~/.ssh/config<br/>hosts, usernames, keys"]
        pers["~/.claude/lab/personal.md<br/>folders, ports, job defaults"]
        key["~/.claude/lab/edison.env<br/>the Edison key"]
    end
    skill -->|"resolves aliases at run time"| ssh
    skill -->|"reads into the agent's context"| pers
    skill -->|"edison-cli sources it into<br/>its process, never into context"| key

tests/lint.sh sweeps every file for a leaked address, hostname or username. It reads your own ssh config to know which names to look for, so the sweep is complete only on a machine with the lab's ssh aliases. CI cannot run it in full, which is why you run the gate before you push.

The Edison key gets a file of its own because personal.md is read into the agent's context. That is its job. A key written there would land in the transcript of every session. The key file is sourced by a shell instead, so the key reaches the client without ever appearing as text.

Read the record: The Edison key gets its own file.

items.title: Rules become structure
items.text:
A rule an agent must remember at the moment it matters fails sooner or later. Where a rule guards something costly, the repo turns it into something that runs.

  • Preflights refuse. lab-hpc checks the machine's ssh setup before any cluster work, and refuses on a machine that is not set up rather than asking for an address.
  • Spending goes through a command. lab-edison once taught an agent to submit a task, print its id, and only then poll. A real session lost a paid run's id anyway, and it had to be dug out of the task history. Now edison-cli does it in order:
flowchart TB
    typed["A person types /lab-edison"] --> pre["edison-cli runs its preflight: no key file, no spend"]
    pre --> file["The question goes into a file, which the person sees in full"]
    file --> submit["Submit from that file: the task id is the first line out"]
    submit --> poll["Poll, then fetch the answer"]
  • Lint checks the conventions. Names, version tags, eval case lists and the no-secrets sweep are all checks in tests/lint.sh, not reminders in a document.
  • Some steps always wait for a person. hq-mode's always-pause list, such as submitting a Slurm job or merging an unreviewed pull request, outranks anything said in the session, "land it" included.

Read the records: The Edison skill ships its spend path and The spend path became a package.

items.title: Two kinds of page
items.text:
Every page is written either for an agent that has to act, or for a person reading this site. The gate checks each kind for different things.

For agents For people Files AGENTS.md, every SKILL.md and references/ page, docs/adr/, docs/agents/ README.md, CHANGELOG.md, the pages in this site's menu Checked for A word cap for each kind of file No jargon from the lab's list, and a reading grade of 11 or below On this site Out of the menu and search, still reachable by URL In the menu and search

A cap that fires means the text belongs somewhere else, such as a references/ page, not that the cap should rise. Upstream text in an adopted skill is exempt, so it passes unchanged. docs/agents/writing.md has the caps and how to measure against them.

items.title: Upstream skills keep upstream text
items.text: The lab takes general engineering skills from mattpocock/skills and pstack instead of writing its own. A tracked skill only ever gains text, and keeps its upstream name, so each sync merges cleanly. Skills from mattpocock and pstack has the whole story.

items.title: The docs site runs on an alpha
items.text:
This site is built by zensical, an early 0.0.x builder from the makers of Material for MkDocs. The lab wants every repo on one builder, and this repo is the cheapest place to try it: a few hand-written pages, nothing generated. The pin is exact, and moving back to mkdocs is a short change to pyproject.toml and mkdocs.yml.

Read the record: The docs site is built by zensical.

items.title: Skills from mattpocock and pstack
items.text:
The lab writes the skills that know about its clusters and its platforms. The general engineering skills, for planning, building, reviewing and writing, come from two outside projects:

  • mattpocock/skills, a set of agent skills for planning and building software, such as grilling, to-spec, tdd and code-review.
  • pstack, a skill pack in cursor/plugins. Its poteto-mode and its principles shaped hq-mode, and four of its skills ship here: unslop, technical-writing, ketchup and bro.

Both are MIT licensed. Their licenses sit in upstream/<project>/LICENSE.

items.title: Two projects, two ways in
items.text:
The lab follows both projects, but takes text from each in a different way.

flowchart LR
    mp["mattpocock/skills<br/>pin says: merge"]
    ps["pstack<br/>pin says: review"]
    mp -->|"merged on every sync"| tracked["Tracked skills<br/>upstream text,<br/>plus lab edits that only add"]
    mp -.->|"forked, when merging<br/>costs more than it saves"| forked["Forked skills<br/>owned by the lab"]
    ps -->|"forked from day one"| forked
    ps -->|"taken as ideas, rewritten"| hq["hq-mode pages<br/>playbooks, principles, working style"]

Each project has a pin in upstream/<project>/pin.json: the commit last synced and a map from each upstream item to the lab file it feeds. Every forked item, including each hq-mode page built from pstack, also gets a record in upstream/attribution.json.

mattpocock is merged. Its skills arrive as written, and the lab only ever adds to them. Each sync merges upstream's new text into the lab's copy, so an upstream fix reaches the lab at the next sync.

pstack is only reviewed. Nothing the lab takes from it arrives unchanged: its principles became pages inside hq-mode, and its other items lose text written for Cursor. Most of its churn trims words for the models Cursor runs. The lab runs other agents on other models, so a sync lists what changed in pstack and a person decides what to port by hand.

items.title: Tracked, forked and derived
items.text:
Kind Who owns the text How upstream changes arrive Name Tracked Upstream, plus lab edits that only add Merged by each sync Upstream's own Forked The lab As ideas in the sync's summary, ported by hand Upstream's own Derived The lab, from the start As ideas only lab-*, or hq-mode

Every mattpocock skill starts tracked. The maintainer forks one when merging it costs more than it saves, by judgement and not by a fixed threshold. Every pstack item is forked.

To see which skills are tracked, read the pin's items map:

python3 -c 'import json; print(*json.load(open("upstream/mattpocock/pin.json"))["items"], sep="\n")'

items.title: Adding to a tracked skill
items.text:
A lab edit may add to a tracked skill and may never remove a line of upstream's text. That rule is what lets the next sync merge cleanly. It has two forms:

  • A short branch or a loop path goes in place, in the upstream file.
  • A whole new section goes in a side page beside it, named <topic>.lab.md, with a one-line pointer from the upstream file. For example, skills/code-review/science-smells.lab.md adds the defects that change an analysis result, such as an unseeded random split.

A safety rule is never a lab edit. It goes on hq-mode's always-pause list or into a lab-owned skill, where no upstream change can reword it.

items.title: How a sync runs
items.text:
The maintainer runs /lab-upstream-sync by hand, about once a month. It lives in .claude/commands/, so plugin users never see it.

sequenceDiagram
    actor M as Maintainer
    participant S as Sync command
    participant R as This repo
    M->>S: start on a sync branch
    S->>S: clone both upstreams fresh
    loop each tracked skill, file by file
        S->>R: git merge-file, base = pinned commit
    end
    S-->>M: conflicts, deletions, stale words, lost edits
    S-->>M: what is new in both upstreams
    M->>S: a decision on each item
    S->>R: one pull request, one version bump

The repo stores no copy of upstream, only the pin, and the pull request moves each pin forward. The merge finds a skill by its frontmatter name, so upstream can move a skill between folders at no cost. A deleted upstream skill shows up in the report instead of vanishing.

items.title: Names stay as upstream wrote them
items.text:
An adopted skill keeps its upstream name, typed bare: /grilling, not /lab-grilling. Upstream skills name each other in their text. wayfinder names grilling, research and prototype, so a rename would have to be redone on every sync. A lab-* name therefore marks a skill the lab wrote. tests/lint.sh fails any other name unless upstream/ records it, with hq-mode the one exception.

The cost is shadowing. A bare name reaches whichever skill holds it, so an old copy of grilling in a user's own skills folder wins over the plugin's without a word. /lab-setup lists such copies and removes none.

items.title: What hq-mode took from each
items.text:
hq-mode is the lab's own skill, but most of its shape is borrowed.

flowchart LR
    subgraph from["Where it came from"]
        poteto["pstack poteto-mode"]
        princ["pstack principle-* skills"]
        fio["pstack figure-it-out"]
        verify["pstack show-me-your-work,<br/>verification and benchmark skills"]
        ask["mattpocock ask-matt"]
        lab["The lab's own sessions,<br/>with ideas from pstack's<br/>automate-me and why"]
    end
    subgraph hq["hq-mode"]
        shape["A router over playbooks,<br/>read with principles"]
        code["Code playbooks: land the tickets,<br/>improve a metric, refactor, investigation, long run"]
        pages["Principle pages,<br/>some with lab edits for science"]
        fallback["The fallback playbook,<br/>for a task no playbook fits"]
        refs["Decision log, checks,<br/>benchmark checklist"]
        trig["The trigger table:<br/>which skill comes next"]
        rules["Working-style rules,<br/>the always-pause list,<br/>science and writing playbooks"]
    end
    poteto --> shape
    poteto --> code
    princ --> pages
    fio --> fallback
    verify --> refs
    ask --> trig
    lab --> rules

In pstack each principle is its own skill. Here each is a page that hq-mode reads by path when the principle applies. The science edits are small and named. For example, before an agent trusts a result number, it rules out data leaking between splits, batch effects, repeated samples, and a filter that changed what the number is out of.

items.title: The lab defaults reuse upstream's setup pages
items.text:
mattpocock's planning skills expect three things to be "provided to you": an issue tracker, triage labels and a place for domain docs. Upstream's setup-matt-pocock-skills writes these into each repo. The lab provides them once per machine instead.

flowchart TB
    seed["Upstream's seed pages,<br/>from setup-matt-pocock-skills"] --> defaults["The lab defaults page in lab-setup:<br/>the seed pages, plus lab lines"]
    defaults -->|"/lab-setup points each agent at it"| agent["Every agent on the machine"]
    own["A repo's own docs/agents/ page"] -->|"overrides that one default"| agent

The defaults page links upstream's pages as written and adds the lab's lines, among them the GitHub issue rules for a public repo, the cluster rules that hold in every session, and the line that turns on hq-mode's working style. A repo that differs keeps its own page under docs/agents/, and runs /setup-matt-pocock-skills only for that.

items.title: hq-mode: work through a whole task the lab's way
items.text:
Type it at the start of a task, followed by what you want:

/hq-mode analyse the new run and tell me if the batch effect is gone

It never starts on its own. You turn it on, in Claude Code, Codex or Kimi Code.
path: hq-mode: work through a whole task the lab's way

items.title: What it does
items.text:
First the agent reads one page of working rules. They cover when to ask you and when to find the answer itself, what it may do without asking, how it splits work between helpers, and how it writes its reply. A rule in your repo's own AGENTS.md wins over that page.

Then it picks the playbook that fits your task and copies its steps into its to-do list, so you can see what it will do and how far it has got. An agent with no to-do list puts the steps in its first reply instead. The playbooks:

Kind Playbooks Science analysis, cluster run, method research, experiment plan, figure Writing paper section, grant section, talk, review a document, message, docs page Code land the tickets, improve a metric, refactor analysis code, investigation Any task long run, close the session

When none fits, it designs one for the task, writes the steps down, and works through them.

It also follows a set of working principles. Each is a short page it reads when that principle applies, such as "check the real output, not a sign of it". A few were changed for science work. For example, before it trusts a cell count, it rules out data leaking between splits, batch effects, repeated samples and a filter that changed what the count is out of.

It also knows which skill to reach for along the way: the lab cluster skills before any ssh, unslop before you read its prose, and the planning skills such as /grill-with-docs and /to-spec for a new idea. A skill you start by typing its name stays yours to start. The agent suggests it rather than running it.
path: hq-mode: work through a whole task the lab's way

items.title: What it always asks first
items.text:
Some steps wait for your yes, every time:

  • submitting, running or cancelling a Slurm job, after it shows you the exact script in its reply, not a link to it;
  • spending Edison credits;
  • writing to or deleting from the lab's shared package store;
  • force-pushing, or deleting data;
  • merging a pull request nobody reviewed, unless you told it to land it;
  • anything on a live service;
  • making private work public;
  • wet-lab steps;
  • editing your own document beyond what you asked for.

This list wins over everything else you say in the session. "I'm going to bed, land it" lets the agent keep going on its own. It still stops at a Slurm job and waits for you, and you find the script ready in the morning. "Close the issue" is not "merge it": while the fix is not merged, the agent leaves the issue open and asks you.
path: hq-mode: work through a whole task the lab's way

items.title: Where the rules came from
items.text: They are the lab's way of working, drawn from many real sessions and written as "the user", so they apply to whoever types /hq-mode. Several playbooks build on pstack's poteto-mode, the principles come from pstack too, and the planning flow follows mattpocock/skills. Both are MIT licensed.
path: hq-mode: work through a whole task the lab's way

items.title: lab-containers: Singularity images on ircbc
items.text:
The lab's software environments are built with pixi and published as container images (the liulab-runtime registry). On ircbc they are the only way to run modern software: the cluster's OS is far too old for current tools, and its compute nodes have no internet. So the images are staged as Singularity files (SIFs) in a shared lab store, and this skill teaches the agent the routine.

ircbc only

On arc the same environments run natively under pixi. No containers are needed there.

items.title: What the agent does with it
items.text:
Checks before rebuilding. Every image records the registry version it was built from. Ask for "the ml image, updated" and the agent compares that record against the registry first, then tells you whether an update is really needed. It never rebuilds blindly.

Pulls and builds the offline way. The download runs on the login node, the one place with network. The build then runs as a Slurm job you approve, and the image lands in the shared store.

Smoke-tests the result. After a build the agent repeats the import and version checks the image was built with, in a small test job, and tells you if anything looks off.

Runs your work inside the image. Batch commands, an interactive shell with the environment already active, or Jupyter Lab in the container. For Jupyter it hands the session to lab-jupyter, which sets up the tunnel.

items.title: Why a login node shows up here
items.text: Reading an image from a compute node is fine, because the shared store is mounted there too. Downloading a new one is not, since ircbc compute nodes have no internet at all. That is one of the two cases where lab-hpc lets the agent step onto a login node. It downloads, then goes straight back to the job.

items.title: Shared-store etiquette
items.text: These images belong to the whole group. The agent asks first before it overwrites or deletes anything another lab member may be using, and it keeps the store writable for everyone.

items.title: When it triggers
items.text: "Pull/build/update the … image on ircbc", "is the ml container up to date?", "run this inside the container", "shell into the align-rna environment".

items.title: lab-edison: cited answers from the Edison platform
items.text: Edison is a research platform, run by Edison Scientific. It answers questions from the published literature with citations, runs code on a dataset you upload, and in Kosmos has a research agent that works a whole goal over many rounds. This skill drives it from your machine through edison-cli, a command that ships with the plugin. No cluster is involved. It is the one skill here that talks only to a cloud service.
path: lab-edison: cited answers from the Edison platform

items.title: You ask for it by name
items.text:
The skill never loads on its own. The other three trigger from what you say; this one waits.

/lab-edison what is known about ...

Anything else you would put to a researcher goes after that same command: "Has anyone already done this experiment?", "Analyse this table and tell me what it shows", "Set up my Edison key on this machine."

Every run spends credits from your own account. That is why nothing here starts without you.

Other agent tools

Claude Code and Kimi Code both honour the setting that holds the skill back. Codex ignores it. It reads a small opt-out file instead, agents/openai.yaml, which ships beside the skill. So in all three the skill waits for you. In any other tool it may load on its own, but it still refuses to run without a key, and it still shows you the job before it sends one.
path: lab-edison: cited answers from the Edison platform

items.title: Your key, and where it goes
items.text:
You need an Edison API key. It lives in one file on your own machine, ~/.claude/lab/edison.env:

mkdir -p ~/.claude/lab
printf 'export EDISON_PLATFORM_API_KEY=PASTE-YOUR-EDISON-KEY-HERE\n' \
  > ~/.claude/lab/edison.env
chmod 600 ~/.claude/lab/edison.env

Then open the file in your editor and paste your key over the placeholder. You do not have to remember any of this: when something is missing, the check the skill runs first prints those exact commands back to you. templates/edison.env is the same file with the reasoning in its comments. The variable name is the one the client reads and no other, and the chmod leaves the file readable by you alone.

The key sits beside personal.md, never inside it. An agent reads personal.md into the chat, so a key written there would be copied into every transcript you ever record.

Before it does anything, the skill checks that file. If it is missing, still holds the placeholder, or is readable by other people, the agent stops and says which check failed. It offers to write the file for you, with the placeholder in place, and then hands it back to you. It will never ask you to type or paste your key into the chat.
path: lab-edison: cited answers from the Edison platform

items.title: What happens before it spends
items.text:
You see the job and the query. The skill names the job it picked and prints your question in full, before the task goes out.

The costly runs stop and ask: a deep literature run, a data analysis run, and any batch of more than three tasks. A follow-up rides on the run you just read, instead of paying again for the same background.

No prices appear anywhere in this repo. They change, and a stale number is worse than none at all. Check the balance on the platform when the cost matters.
path: lab-edison: cited answers from the Edison platform

items.title: A run takes minutes, and the id is the receipt
items.text:
Edison runs are slow enough that nobody should sit and watch one. The skill sends the task, prints the task id straight away, and then checks on it. You get your terminal back.

That id outlives the session that made it. If your laptop sleeps, the window closes, or the agent stops early, the run carries on and finishes on the platform. So a run is never really lost: the skill can list the tasks on your account, newest first, and find the one you started. It offers to do that before asking the same question twice, because asking twice means paying twice for an answer you already own. It can also cancel a run you started by mistake, which is worth knowing before a long data analysis job.
path: lab-edison: cited answers from the Edison platform

items.title: Kosmos, for a goal rather than a question
items.text:
Kosmos is the platform's heavyweight agent, and the reason to come here when what you have is bigger than one query. It is not a task you send off. You pick a persona, make a project inside it, and talk to it there. Kosmos splits your goal into many smaller tasks and works through them in rounds until it decides it is done. One real project ran thirteen of them.

That shape is also what makes it cost. A run pays for every task it fans out to, so there is no flat price to quote, and the skill will not start one unless you ask for that run in plain words.

Everything it does around a run is free. It drafts the goal with you, checks your data is in a shape Kosmos can use, and shows you a run you already started, task by task, without opening a browser.
path: lab-edison: cited answers from the Edison platform

items.title: Names, not long ids
items.text:
The platform gives every persona and project a long random id. You do not have to keep track of them. Say the name, and the skill finds the id for you. If nothing matches that name, it stops and says so. If more than one thing matches, it stops and lists them all with their ids. It never guesses.

Names it has looked up are kept in a small file next to your key. That file holds names and ids and nothing else. Anything that spends money, or removes something, skips it and asks the platform again. So a name that has since moved to a different project cannot point the skill at the wrong one.

Deleting a project is the one step here you cannot undo. The skill prints the project, its name and how many runs it holds, and asks whether the run history goes with it. Nothing is removed until you say yes.
path: lab-edison: cited answers from the Edison platform

items.title: One question, one job
items.text:
For a single question the skill picks one of the platform's one-shot jobs and routes to it.

You are asking What it picks A question the published papers can answer, with citations The literature job The same, but the papers disagree and it needs real reasoning The deeper literature job, slower and dearer Has anyone done this before? The precedent job Chemistry: molecules, properties, how to make one The molecules job Something about a dataset you supply The analysis job

Ask in plain words and the skill picks for you. Say which one you want and it uses that.
path: lab-edison: cited answers from the Edison platform

items.title: Where your data sits
items.text: Your own machine, by default, because that is where your key belongs. Data on your laptop uploads and runs with nothing to arrange. Data on a cluster comes down first and uploads from here, so your key stays off shared hardware. You can run Edison on arc, but only after you put the key there yourself, in your own session. The skill never copies your key anywhere: not to a cluster, not into a job script, not onto a command line.
path: lab-edison: cited answers from the Edison platform

items.title: What it needs, and why the first run waits
items.text:
You need pixi on your machine. It is the only extra tool this skill asks for, and no other skill here asks for it.

Nothing else has to be installed. The first Edison command builds the environment it runs in, and dozens of packages download before your question is even sent. It can look hung. It is not.

That environment lives inside the plugin's own folder, not in any project of yours. An update puts the new version of the plugin in a fresh folder, so the build runs once more after each update. It is quicker then, because the downloads are already on your disk.
path: lab-edison: cited answers from the Edison platform

items.title: lab-hpc: clusters, Slurm, and safety
items.text: The foundation skill. It loads before any ssh or Slurm work and hands the agent the lab's cluster map, the workflow, and the hard safety rules. The other cluster skills build on it.

items.title: The two clusters
items.text:
arc (chimera) ircbc Hardware GPU cluster, H100 nodes CPU cluster Software Recent OS; pixi runs natively CentOS 7, so modern tools need Singularity containers Access ssh alias arc or chimera-login ssh alias ircbc, behind a VPN you start by hand Lab perks Free zhoulab_gpu_priority partition, plus free preemptible tiers Shared store of prebuilt container images

Which cluster fits a task is your call. The agent asks, or reads the answer from your request. It never picks one in silence.

items.title: What the skill enforces
items.text:
Preflight first. The agent checks that your ~/.ssh/config defines the lab aliases, and reports a line per cluster: arc_hpc is arc, ircbc_hpc is ircbc. If the one you need is missing, it refuses the request and points you at the setup steps. It never asks you for a raw address or a password.

Work belongs on a compute node. A login node is a doorway, not a workspace: one shared machine per cluster, and a crowd of agents each firing off "small" commands is what brings it down. So ssh arc '<command>' is the wrong move even for a one-liner, and it is rarely needed, because squeue, sbatch and scancel all run from the compute node anyway.

Two reasons to touch a login node, and no others. Either you hold no job yet, and only a login node can submit the first one. Or the compute node truly lacks something: on ircbc that means internet access and git, and on arc it means nothing at all. The arc compute nodes have their own internet and a full toolchain, so once you land on one, stay.

Reuse the idle job. The lab parks a long-lived idle GPU job on arc, so a node is usually waiting for you. The agent finds it with squeue and works there. If no job is running anywhere, it offers to start one first.

Show before submit. You see the exact sbatch or srun before it runs.

Stop at a down VPN. If ircbc does not answer, the agent asks you to check the VPN rather than retrying in a loop.

items.title: The workflow it follows
items.text: Code is written on your own machine and travels through GitHub: edit, git push, then git pull on the cluster, then run on a compute node. The agent knows the usual code directory on each cluster, and reads your own settings from ~/.claude/lab/personal.md.

items.title: When it triggers
items.text: Any mention of the clusters or of remote compute: ssh to a lab server, Slurm commands (sbatch, srun, squeue), GPU or compute nodes, moving files to a cluster, testing code remotely.

items.title: lab-jupyter: notebooks on the cluster
items.text: Gets a Jupyter Lab running on a cluster compute node and makes it reachable at http://localhost:<port> in your local browser. It works on either cluster.

items.title: How a session goes
items.text:
1. Reuse before submit. The agent lists your running jobs first. If you already have a Jupyter job or an idle reservation, it works on that node instead of queueing a new one, and it asks before borrowing a reservation.
  2. Submit with your approval. Otherwise it drafts a Slurm job, asks which resources you want, and shows you the exact command before submitting. On arc that runs your own Jupyter install; on ircbc it runs inside the lab's container image.
  3. Token. It fishes the login URL and token out of the job's log.
  4. Tunnel. It opens a background ssh tunnel to the compute node and checks that the tunnel works. Then it hands you the full http://localhost:<port>/lab?token=… link.
  5. Cleanup when you ask. It kills the tunnel. It cancels the job only after asking, and it never cancels a job it did not start.

items.title: What differs between the clusters
items.text:
On arc your own Jupyter, named in personal.md, runs in a job on the free zhoulab_gpu_priority partition. Pick this side for GPU work.

On ircbc Jupyter lives inside the lab's Singularity image, described in lab-containers. The agent uses the container launch command, and the cluster's older Slurm dialect, without being told.

items.title: Fewer questions
items.text: The agent asks the usual ones before it submits, listed under basic usage. Fill in ~/.claude/lab/personal.md and most of them go away: it holds your port (9990 by default), the path to your Jupyter on arc, and the resources you usually ask for.

items.title: When it triggers
items.text: "Jupyter on the cluster", "notebook on a GPU node", "tunnel to a compute node", "reconnect to my Jupyter job".

items.title: lab-setup: one step after installing
items.text:
Type it once on each machine, in Claude Code, right after the two install commands on the home page:

/lab-setup

From then on Claude Code, Codex and Kimi Code all use the lab skills, and all three keep them up to date without you running anything. edison-cli works in all three as well.

items.title: What it sets up
items.text:
• Claude Code updates the plugin by itself. It checks in the background while you work, and a new release loads the next time you start it.
  • Codex gets the same plugin, and checks for a new release each time it starts.
  • Kimi Code reads the skills from the copy Claude Code keeps up to date, so it follows every Claude Code update.
  • edison-cli gets a link in ~/.local/bin or ~/bin, whichever your shell already searches, so the command works outside Claude Code too.
  • The lab's defaults reach all three agents. Each agent's own notes file gets a short block that points at one page in the plugin. That page says where a repo's issues go, which labels to use, and the safety rules for the clusters. So a new repo needs no setup, and a change to the page reaches every agent with the next update.

If you don't have Codex or Kimi Code, it skips that part and says so.

It runs a small Python script, which needs Python 3.11 or newer. A fresh Mac has an older one. There the agent runs it through pixi instead, which lab-edison needs anyway.

items.title: It asks first, and removes nothing
items.text:
The agent shows you every change before it makes one, and asks about each. You can say no to any of them. Nothing on your machine is deleted, and a setting you wrote yourself stays as it was.

Running it again is safe. On a machine that is already set up it changes nothing, and on a machine that is half set up it finishes the job.

items.title: Your own notes files
items.text:
The block goes at the end of ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, ~/.codex/AGENTS.md and ~/.kimi-code/AGENTS.md, between two marker lines. Text outside the markers is yours and stays as you wrote it. A second run replaces only what sits between them.

If you once pasted the lab's safety rules into ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md by hand, you can delete that section now. The defaults page carries the same rules, and Codex and Kimi Code get them too.

items.title: Old copies of the same skills
items.text: You call a skill by its plain name, so an old copy in your own skills folder can win over the plugin's copy without a word. /lab-setup lists every such copy and where it lives. It leaves them alone: what to do with each one is your call. If you once installed skills with npx skills, those are the copies to remove.

items.title: Updating by hand
items.text:
You don't need to. If you want a release before your agent picks it up:

claude plugin marketplace update liulab
claude plugin update lab@liulab

Then restart Claude Code.
